pl-l3d9c1-d1e117.summary: Asks whether Christ's flesh and soul should be adored with one and the same adoration as the Word, namely latria, the service or worship due to the Creator alone. If latria is given to Christ's soul or flesh, which are only creatures, what is owed to the Creator alone is given to a creature, which counts as idolatry.
claims: Latria is owed to the Creator alone.
Giving latria to a creature is idolatry.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e120.summary: Reports a first view: Christ's flesh or soul is adored not with latria but with dulia, which has two kinds: one that can be shown to any creature, another shown only to Christ's humanity, which is to be venerated and loved above every creature, but not with the worship due to divinity, consisting in love, sacrifice, and reverence, called pietas in Latin, theosebia or eusebia in Greek.
claims: On one view, Christ's humanity receives a special dulia, not latria.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e123.summary: Reports a second view: Christ's humanity is adored with one adoration with the Word, not for itself but for him whose footstool it is and to whom it is united, not alone or bare but with the Word. One who does this is not guilty of idolatry, since he serves not a creature alone or for its own sake, but the Creator with and in his humanity.
claims: Christ's humanity is adored with the Word, for the Word's sake.
This is not idolatry.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e127.summary: Cites John Damascene: Christ's two natures differ but are united in hypostasis; we adore one Christ, perfect God and perfect man, with the Father and Spirit, with one adoration together with his flesh, not as bare flesh but united to deity in the one hypostasis of the Word. I fear to touch the coal because of the fire joined to the wood; I adore both together because of the deity united to the flesh, not adding a fourth person to the Trinity.
claims: Christ's flesh is adored as united to the deity in one hypostasis.
Adoring Christ's flesh does not add a fourth person.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e133.summary: Observes that Damascene's words suggest Christ's humanity is adored with one adoration with the Word.
claims: Christ's humanity is adored with one adoration with the Word.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e136.summary: Cites Augustine on 'Let not your heart be troubled' (Jn 14:1): heretics say the Son is not God by nature but a creature; if so, he should neither be worshipped nor adored as God, since the Apostle condemns those who served the creature rather than the Creator (Rom 1:25).
claims: If the Son were a creature, he should not be adored.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e151.summary: Continues Augustine with the heretics' reply: why then do you adore his flesh, which you admit is a creature, together with his divinity, serving it no less than the divinity?
claims: Objection: adoring Christ's flesh is adoring a creature.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e157.summary: Gives Augustine's answer: I adore the Lord's flesh, indeed his whole humanity, because it was assumed by and united to the deity, so that I confess one and the same Son, God and man. If you separate the man from God I neither believe nor serve him. As one would not adore royal purple or a diadem lying on the ground, but risks death if he refuses to adore them when the king wears them, so whoever refuses to adore Christ's humanity, united to divinity, will die eternally.
claims: Christ's humanity is adored because united to the deity.
Separated from God, the man would not be adored.
Refusing to adore Christ's united humanity is damnable.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e163.summary: Cites Augustine on Ps 98:5, 'adore his footstool': in Christ the earth is the flesh, which is adored without impiety; he took earth from earth, flesh from Mary's flesh. No one eats his flesh unless he first adores it; but one who adores looks not to the earth but to him whose footstool it is.
claims: Christ's flesh is adored without impiety.
The adorer looks to the one whose footstool it is.

pl-l3d9c1-d1e179.summary: Concludes that these authorities resolve the question raised.
claims: The authorities resolve the question in favor of one adoration.

pl-l3d9c1.summary: Asks whether Christ's flesh and soul should be adored with the same adoration as the Word, latria, owed to the Creator alone, since giving it to a creature is idolatry. Some say Christ's humanity receives dulia, of a special kind owed to it alone above all creatures, but not the worship (pietas, theosebia, eusebia) due to God. Others say it is adored with one adoration with the Word, not for itself or bare, but as united to the Word; this is not idolatry. Damascene (the coal joined to fire), Augustine on 'Let not your heart be troubled' (the royal purple worn by the king), and Augustine on Ps 98 (adore his footstool) settle the question in favor of one adoration of Christ's humanity with the Word.
claims: Latria is owed to the Creator alone.
Some hold Christ's humanity receives a special dulia.
Christ's humanity is adored with one adoration with the Word, as united to it.
Adoring Christ's humanity with the Word is not idolatry.
